title: The enemy of my enemy
hook: The enemy of my enemy is my friend. How far does that saying go?

knows: the saying "the enemy of my enemy is my friend"
doesNotKnow: that if every group of three is balanced, the whole group must split into at most two camps

misconception: A friend-and-enemy network can settle into several mutually hostile camps (three or more), or the saying alone does not say how many camps there can be.
objective: The learner can explain that when every trio of a fully connected friend/enemy group is balanced, the group is one camp or two (friends inside, enemies across), because three camps always contain a trio of three enemies: on five people, 3 camps leave at least 3 unbalanced trios.

claims.text: A trio is balanced if it has three friend (+) pairs, or one friend pair and two enemy (−) pairs; equivalently, its three signs multiply to +.
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 5 §5.1 (§ unconfirmed: from the table of contents, the book page returned a proxy 403 to the category manager). Code: unbalancedTrios() in src/demos/math/enemy-of-my-enemy/Demo.tsx (product of the three signs < 0). Address: predict question, stage rule line.

claims.text: Among the 1,024 friend/enemy settings of five people (10 pairs), 16 have every trio balanced: 1 is one camp (all friends) and 15 are two camps; every one of the 16 is a clean camp split (friends inside, enemies across).
claims.source: Node enumeration of all 2^10 sign settings with the lesson's exact rule (builder script, session scratchpad eme-check.mjs; brief 2 check by cm-math-discrete gives the same 16 = 2^(5-1)). Output: balanced 16, one camp 1, two camps 15, balanced but not a camp split 0. Address: reveal paragraph 3 ('one camp or two') for five people.

claims.text: In a camp split, the only unbalanced trios are those with one person from each of three different camps: such a trio has three enemy pairs. A trio inside one camp is + + +, and a trio with two in one camp is one + and two −, both balanced.
claims.source: Case analysis of the definition (c1); confirmed by node over all camp splits of 5 people. Address: reveal paragraph 2 ('one person from each camp makes a trio of three enemies').

claims.text: With five people in three non-empty camps, at least 3 trios are unbalanced: a 3-1-1 split leaves 3 and a 2-2-1 split leaves 4. Four camps leave 7, and all enemies (five camps) leaves all 10.
claims.source: Node enumeration over all 3^5 camp labellings with three non-empty camps (3-1-1: 3; 2-2-1: 4) and over all camp splits of the 1,024 settings (unbalanced by number of camps: 1 → 0, 2 → 0, 3 → 3 or 4, 4 → 7, 5 → 10). Address: reveal paragraph 2 ('at least 3', 'all 10'); stage readout 'Unbalanced'.

claims.text: On the stage, the '3 camps' preset is ABC | D | E with 3 of 10 trios unbalanced, and flipping D–E to friends makes ABC | DE with 0; starting from all enemies (10 unbalanced), making A–B, B–C, A–C friends gives ABC | D | E (3), and then D–E gives ABC | DE (0).
claims.source: Node replay of the QA path with the lesson's rules (scratchpad eme-check.mjs): start 10; AB 7 (AB|C|D|E); BC 6 (mixed); AC 3 (ABC|D|E); DE 0 (ABC|DE); AD 3; AE 4; BD 5; BE 4; CD 3 (all mixed); CE 0 (ABCDE); preset 3 camps 3 (ABC|D|E). Address: reveal paragraph 1 quotes the learner's own reached states.

claims.text: Balance theorem: if every trio of a complete friend/enemy network is balanced, then either everyone is friends or the people split into two groups, friends inside and enemies across; it holds for any number of people, and is due to Cartwright and Harary (1956).
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010) ch. 5 §5.2 (§ unconfirmed), which attributes the result to Harary and to Cartwright and Harary (1956): D. Cartwright and F. Harary, 'Structural balance: a generalization of Heider's theory', Psychological Review 63(5), 277-293 (1956). Attribution and year unverified by the builder (could not open the source); the fact-checker confirms. Not empirical; the n = 5 case is checked by enumeration (c2). Address: reveal paragraph 3.

recall.question: Six countries; every pair is allied or hostile, and every trio is balanced. Can they form three blocs, allied inside and hostile to every other bloc?
options: Yes, if the blocs are equal in size
Yes, any number of blocs works
recall.why: Take one country from each of three blocs: all three pairs are hostile, and a trio of three enemies is unbalanced. So balance allows one bloc or two, never three.
